newsitem.title: USA: Judge has doubts over N.Y.'s plan for Fox.
newsitem.headline: Judge has doubts over N.Y.'s plan for Fox.

text.p: A federal judge raised doubts Monday that New York City can legally proceed with its plan to air Rupert Murdoch's Fox News Network or any commercial programming on its city-run cable stations.

U.S. District Judge Denise Cote, who previously granted Time Warner's request for a temporary order halting efforts by Mayor Rudolph Giuliani to run the Fox 24-hour news channel, outlined concerns during a hearing on a permanent bar.
The hearing is to continue Tuesday.

The dispute centers on the role of the city's five stations, known as Crosswalks. Giuliani decided to place the new Fox channel on one of the of the Crosswalks channels after Time Warner rejected it. He also plans to run Bloomberg Television News, which also is not aired by Time Warner.

Time Warner, which serves 1.1 million customers in New York, sued the city alleging that Giuliani was acting on behalf of Murdoch's News Corp. Ltd., which owns the New York Post and WNYW-TV. It said in its suit that the city was acting as Murdoch's "latest political puppet."

At issue is whether the city's plan violates its franchise agreement with Time Warner and the Federal Cable Act that limits what can be shown on public, educational and governmental, known as PEG, access channels.

Time Warner alleges the franchise agreements provide that the city-run channels be used for non-commercial purposes and that the federal law also prohibits the governmental stations from being used for commercial programming.
The city argues that such use is not strictly prohibited and that is has often transmitted commercial programming.
During Monday's hearing, Cote said she was troubled by the city's definition of the term "governmental use."
"In essence, the city is arguing that if the city chooses to put any particular programming on Crosswalks for any reason whatsoever, that is an appropriate use of Crosswalks.

"It also appears from the position the city is taking with respect to Bloomberg and Fox News that the city intends to transform Crosswalks to incorporate commercial programming to compete with Time Warner's programming whenever it disagrees with the decisions Time Warner has made with respect to programming on the commercial stations."
She said she had doubts that the government could use such a channel to compete with a commercial cable operator.

"I'm not sure that that's consistent with the Cable Act or with the Constitution," she said. However she added that there was no agreement among the parties about the definition of "commercial use" and that this presented a complex question.

Rory Millson, a lawyer with Cravath Swaine & Moore, which is representing Time Warner told the judge that the city had recently changed its view that it could run news programs as long as the commercials were removed. He said that now the city's policy, as stated in its legal briefs, is that it can run programming containing commercials.
"They can run anything they want with any commercials they want," he said.
He also argued that the city's move violated Time Warner's free speech rights because it is infringing on its editorial discretion by trying to force it to carry the two news channels.

Paul Crotty, the city's corporation counsel, argued that Time Warner might have to make some business changes due to the city's decision to air the Fox and Bloomberg programming, but its constitutional rights would not be hurt.
"I think I heard cash registers ringing in the background. This might be an injury, but it's not a First Amendment injury," Crotty said.
